findings.lesson_title: Visual Illusions and Gregory's Constructivist Theory
findings.claim: The arrow fins resemble the inside corner of a room (inward, appearing further away) or the outside corner of a building (outward, appearing closer).
findings.issue: The fin-type/corner-type associations are reversed. Inward-pointing fins (>---<) resemble the OUTSIDE corner of a building (protruding toward you = closer), not the inside corner of a room. Outward-pointing fins (<---->) resemble the INSIDE corner of a room (receding from you = further away). The result stated is correct (inward-fin line looks shorter) but the parenthetical Gregory explanation is inverted. An exam answer using this explanation would lose marks.
findings.verified_fact: Gregory's explanation: outward fins (<---->) = inside corner of a room = appears further away → size constancy makes it look LONGER. Inward fins (>---<) = outside corner of a building = appears closer → size constancy makes it look SHORTER. Source: Gregory, R.L. (1968). Perceptual illusions and brain models. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 171, 279-296.
findings.suggested_fix: Change to: 'Gregory's explanation: the inward fins (>---<) resemble the outside corner of a building (appearing closer); because of size constancy, the brain judges the line as shorter. The outward fins (<---->) resemble the inside corner of a room (appearing further away); size constancy then makes the brain judge that line as longer.'

findings.lesson_title: Obedience: Milgram and the Authoritarian Personality
findings.claim: [The lesson covers Milgram's Agency Theory and social/dispositional factors but contains no description of Milgram's actual procedure, no 65% obedience figure, no 450V shock generator detail, and no statement of the baseline study method.]
findings.issue: The AQA 8182 specification requires students to know Milgram's study in full (aim, procedure, findings, conclusion). The lesson teaches Agency Theory and obedience factors but omits the study itself. Students cannot answer standard exam questions such as 'Describe Milgram's study of obedience' or cite the headline finding that 65% of participants administered the maximum 450V shock. Every AQA mark scheme for Milgram awards marks specifically for the 65%/450V statistics. This is a content gap that constitutes a HIGH-severity issue for exam performance.
findings.verified_fact: Milgram (1963): Participants were told to administer electric shocks (15V–450V, 30 increments) to a 'learner' (confederate) for wrong answers. The experimenter used four prods ('please continue', 'the experiment requires you to continue', 'it is absolutely essential that you continue', 'you have no other choice'). 65% of participants (26/40) administered the maximum 450V shock in the baseline condition. Source: Milgram, S. (1963). Behavioral study of obedience. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 67(4), 371–378.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a Key Fact box with Milgram's study: Aim — to investigate whether ordinary people would obey an authority figure's instruction to harm an innocent person. Method — 40 male participants instructed to administer electric shocks (up to 450V in 30 increments) to a confederate learner; four verbal prods used when participants hesitated. Results — 65% of participants continued to the maximum 450V; all participants gave at least 300V. Conclusion — people obey authority figures even when ordered to cause serious harm to others, supporting the idea of an agentic state.

findings.claim: [The lesson discusses STM duration of '15 to 30 seconds' and references Murdock for serial position evidence, but does not name Peterson and Peterson (1959) as the key study for STM duration.]
findings.issue: The AQA 8182 specification lists Peterson and Peterson (1959) as a named study that students must know for STM duration. The lesson mentions the 15–30 second figure as an established fact but attributes no study to it, meaning students cannot answer questions asking them to describe the evidence for STM duration. This is a content gap, not a factual error, but it is HIGH severity for exam purposes because the study is named in the spec.
findings.verified_fact: Peterson & Peterson (1959): Participants were given a trigram (e.g. CHJ) and immediately performed a counting task to prevent rehearsal. Recall was tested after 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 or 18 seconds. After 18 seconds, recall fell to approximately 5%, demonstrating that STM duration is around 18–30 seconds without rehearsal. Source: Peterson, L.R. & Peterson, M.J. (1959). Short-term retention of individual verbal items. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 58(3), 193–198.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a named study section for Peterson & Peterson (1959): Aim — to investigate the duration of STM without rehearsal. Method — participants given a trigram and immediately required to count backwards (preventing rehearsal); recall tested after 3–18 seconds. Results — recall dropped sharply; after 18 seconds only ~5% of items were recalled. Conclusion — STM duration is approximately 18–30 seconds without rehearsal.

findings.claim: [The psychological theory section describes 'negative schemas and attributions' and an attribution style (internal, stable, global), but does not name Beck's Cognitive Triad.]
findings.issue: The AQA 8182 spec requires students to know Beck's Cognitive Triad (negative view of self, negative view of the world, negative view of the future) as the key cognitive model of depression. The lesson describes attribution style and negative schemas accurately but does not use the term 'cognitive triad' or identify the three components. Students cannot answer 'Describe Beck's cognitive triad' questions. The attribution style described (internal/stable/global) is actually from Abramson et al.'s helplessness model, not Beck — conflating the two without naming either is potentially misleading.
findings.verified_fact: Beck's Cognitive Triad (1979): negative view of (1) the self ('I am worthless'), (2) the world ('the world is harsh and unforgiving'), and (3) the future ('things will never get better'). These three components together maintain depression. Source: Beck, A.T. (1979). Cognitive therapy and the emotional disorders. New York: Meridian.
findings.suggested_fix: Name Beck's Cognitive Triad explicitly: 'Aaron Beck proposed that depression is maintained by a cognitive triad — a negative view of the self ("I am worthless"), the world ("things always go wrong") and the future ("things will never improve"). These three negative perspectives reinforce each other and drive the depressive state.' Retain the attribution style content but attribute it to Abramson et al. or frame it separately.

findings.claim: Gilchrist and Nesberg: participants who had gone without food or water for varying lengths of time were shown images of food and drink and asked to adjust the brightness of the images to match what they had seen.
findings.issue: The description is partly accurate but the procedure detail is imprecise. In Gilchrist & Nesberg (1952), participants were shown images of food/drink and then the images were darkened; participants adjusted the brightness to match the remembered original. The key manipulation was deprivation level (hours without food/water), not just 'varying lengths of time' generically. More importantly, the lesson says participants adjusted brightness 'to match what they had seen' — the actual result was that deprived participants set the brightness HIGHER than the actual original, overestimating the brightness of need-relevant stimuli. The lesson's results section correctly says 'adjusted the brightness of food and drink images to appear brighter than less deprived participants did', which captures this, but the method description misleads by framing it as a matching task when it was actually an overestimation.
findings.verified_fact: Gilchrist & Nesberg (1952): Participants were deprived of food/water for 1, 3, 9, or 16 hours. They were shown projected images of food/drink at a standard luminance, then the image was turned off and they adjusted a control to reproduce what they thought they'd seen. Deprived participants set the luminance HIGHER than the original — they did not merely match, they overestimated brightness. Source: Gilchrist, J.C. & Nesberg, L.S. (1952). Need and perceptual change in need-related objects. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 44(5), 369–376.
findings.suggested_fix: Revise method description: 'participants who had been deprived of food or water for varying lengths of time (1–16 hours) were shown images of food and drink at a fixed brightness, then asked to adjust the brightness of the image to reproduce what they had seen.' In the results, retain 'adjusted to appear brighter' and clarify this represents overestimation of the original.

findings.claim: In some conditions the victim appeared drunk (carrying a bottle in a bag); in others they appeared ill (carrying a walking cane).
findings.issue: Minor procedure inaccuracy. In Piliavin et al. (1969), the drunk confederate carried a liquor bottle wrapped in a brown paper bag AND smelled of alcohol. The ill confederate carried a black cane. The lesson omits the alcohol smell detail, which is part of the experimental manipulation that affects the cost-benefit calculation (drunk = harder to help, potentially aggressive). This detail matters for evaluation questions about ecological validity and cost. More significantly, the lesson says 'carrying a bottle in a bag' without mentioning the smell — the smell was what primarily distinguished the conditions in terms of cost to the helper.
findings.verified_fact: Piliavin et al. (1969): The 'ill' confederate carried a black cane; the 'drunk' confederate carried a bottle of alcohol in a brown bag AND smelled of alcohol. Help rates: ill victim received help 95% of the time, drunk victim 50% of the time. The ill victim was helped within 70 seconds in over 90% of trials. Source: Piliavin, I.M., Rodin, J. & Piliavin, J.A. (1969). Good Samaritanism: An underground phenomenon? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 13(4), 289–299.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the smell detail: 'the drunk victim carried a bottle of alcohol in a brown paper bag and smelled of alcohol; the ill victim carried a black cane.' Also consider adding the specific help rates (95% vs 50%) to allow students to cite statistics in exam answers.

findings.claim: Whorf studied the Hopi language and argued that its different treatment of time and events — compared to English — meant Hopi speakers might experience and conceptualise time differently from English speakers.
findings.issue: This description is accurate as far as it goes, but should be more clearly flagged as contested or discredited. Malotki (1983) undertook extensive fieldwork with Hopi speakers and documented that Hopi does in fact have tense and temporal expressions — directly refuting Whorf's specific claim. The lesson says 'subsequent research has challenged some of Whorf's specific claims,' which handles this responsibly, but could be stronger: the Hopi time claim is now considered an error in Whorf's analysis, not merely 'challenged.' AQA examiners expect students to be able to evaluate the hypothesis using this evidence.
findings.verified_fact: Whorf's (1956) claim that Hopi is 'timeless' was refuted by Malotki (1983) who showed Hopi has past/present/future tense markers and extensive time vocabulary. The Hopi-time claim is now widely considered incorrect. However, the broader weak version of linguistic relativity has support from Boroditsky (2001) and others on colour terms and spatial cognition. Source: Malotki, E. (1983). Hopi Time: A Linguistic Analysis of the Temporal Concepts in the Hopi Language. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
findings.suggested_fix: Revise to: 'Whorf claimed that the Hopi language lacked tense, leading him to argue that Hopi speakers conceptualised time differently from English speakers. However, subsequent linguistic research — particularly by Malotki (1983) — found that Hopi does have tense and extensive time vocabulary, casting serious doubt on this specific claim. The general weak version of linguistic relativity (that language influences but does not determine thought) continues to attract empirical support from other areas such as colour naming.'

findings.claim: A round dance indicated that food was close to the hive. A waggle dance (a figure-of-eight pattern with a straight waggle run in the middle) indicated food at a greater distance.
findings.issue: The basic distinction is correct but the distance threshold is missing. Von Frisch established that the round dance is used for food sources within approximately 50–100 metres of the hive, and the waggle dance for distances beyond that. The AQA mark schemes sometimes ask for the specific threshold. Additionally, the lesson doesn't mention that the duration (speed) of the waggle run encodes distance — it says 'duration...corresponded to the distance' but this could be clearer: a shorter waggle run = nearer food; a longer waggle run = further food.
findings.verified_fact: Von Frisch (1967): Round dance = food within ~50–100m. Waggle dance = food beyond ~100m. In the waggle dance, the direction of the straight run relative to vertical corresponds to the direction of the food source relative to the sun; the number of waggles per unit time (or duration of waggle run) encodes distance. Source: von Frisch, K. (1967). The Dance Language and Orientation of Bees. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the distance threshold: 'A round dance indicated food within approximately 50–100 metres of the hive. A waggle dance indicated food at greater distances, with the duration of the waggle run encoding the distance (a longer run = further away) and the angle of the waggle run relative to vertical encoding the direction relative to the sun.'

findings.claim: Male participants were placed in a room with several other people who were actually confederates (actors working for the researcher).
findings.issue: The lesson says 'several other people' without specifying the number. Asch's original study used 7 confederates (making the naïve participant the 8th person). The number matters for evaluation — the group size of 7 was chosen because Asch had established that conformity levels off beyond 3–4, so 7 ensures a strongly unanimous majority. AQA mark schemes sometimes credit specific detail about group size.
findings.verified_fact: Asch's standard procedure used 7 confederates and 1 naïve participant per trial. Source: Asch, S.E. (1951). Effects of group pressure upon the modification and distortion of judgements. In H. Guetzkow (Ed.), Groups, leadership and men (pp. 177–190). Pittsburgh: Carnegie Press.
findings.suggested_fix: Change to 'several other people (typically seven confederates)' to give students the specific group size for exam answers.

findings.claim: The confederates had been instructed to give the same wrong answer on 12 out of 18 trials.
findings.issue: Correct count but terminology could be clearer. These 12 trials are called 'critical trials' — a term AQA mark schemes use. The lesson uses 'critical trials where confederates all gave the wrong answer' later in the results section, which is fine, but having the term in the method description would help students use exam-ready language.
findings.verified_fact: Asch used 18 trials total, of which 12 were 'critical trials' where confederates gave a unanimous wrong answer, and 6 were neutral trials where confederates gave the correct answer. Source: Asch (1951) as above.
findings.suggested_fix: Change to: 'The confederates had been instructed to give the same wrong answer on 12 out of 18 trials (the critical trials).'

findings.claim: Murdock's (1962) investigation of the serial position effect. Aim — to investigate the serial position effect in free recall. Method — participants heard lists of words at a set rate and were asked to recall them in any order immediately after.
findings.issue: The lesson omits the specific list lengths and presentation rates used by Murdock, which AQA mark schemes often credit. Murdock (1962) used lists of 10, 15, 20, 30, and 40 words presented at 1 or 2 words per second. The most commonly cited version for AQA is 20 words at 1 per second. Without these specifics, students cannot give the detailed procedure description required for higher-mark exam answers.
findings.verified_fact: Murdock, B.B. (1962). The serial position effect of free recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64(5), 482–488. Used 240 participants; list lengths of 10, 15, 20, 30, 40 words; presentation rates of 1 or 2 words/second. Most frequently cited version for AQA: 20 words at 1 per second.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to method: 'participants heard lists of words (typically 20 words, presented at a rate of one per second) and were asked to recall them in any order immediately afterwards.'

findings.claim: Antidepressants are effective for many people, quick-acting relative to talking therapies, widely accessible and can be taken independently.
findings.issue: Calling antidepressants 'quick-acting relative to talking therapies' is potentially misleading. SSRIs typically take 2–4 weeks to show therapeutic effect (sometimes 6–8 weeks for full effect). While this is faster than a full course of CBT (usually 12–20 sessions), 'quick-acting' is not an accurate characterisation of antidepressants in absolute terms. AQA mark schemes accept 'faster than CBT' as a comparative strength, but students should understand the absolute timeline.
findings.verified_fact: SSRIs typically take 2–6 weeks to produce noticeable mood improvement; full therapeutic benefit can take 8–12 weeks. Source: NHS (2021). Antidepressants — Overview. https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/medicines-and-psychiatry/antidepressants/overview/
findings.suggested_fix: Revise to: 'Antidepressants typically take 2–6 weeks to have their full effect, which is faster than a full course of CBT, and they are widely accessible — a GP can prescribe them without a long waiting list.'

findings.claim: Piaget proposed that all children pass through four stages in the same order. The age ranges are approximate, but the sequence is fixed.
findings.issue: No factual error — stage ages given (0-2, 2-7, 7-11, 11+) are Piaget's own published ranges and match AQA expectations. The caveat that ages are approximate is accurate and appropriate. However, the lesson does not mention that Piaget's own age estimates have been criticised as conservative — a commonly expected evaluation point at AQA. This is a minor omission, not an error.
findings.verified_fact: Piaget's stage ages: sensorimotor 0–2, pre-operational 2–7, concrete operational 7–11, formal operational 11+. These are the ages published in Piaget (1954) and used universally in AQA resources. Research by McGarrigle & Donaldson and Hughes suggests children achieve concrete operational abilities earlier (~4–6 for conservation with natural tasks). The lesson covers these challenges in L03, so the overall treatment is balanced.
findings.suggested_fix: No change required for the ages themselves. Optionally add one sentence: 'However, critics argue Piaget underestimated children's abilities at each stage — they may pass some tasks earlier when the method is more child-friendly.'

findings.claim: Dopamine is involved in the brain's reward system — it is released when we experience something pleasurable or achieve a goal, reinforcing the behaviour.
findings.issue: Accurate but the link between dopamine and reinforcement in addiction (needed for Psychological Problems L04) is not explicitly made here. More importantly, the lesson says dopamine is released 'when we experience something pleasurable' — neuroscience has refined this to 'dopamine is released in anticipation of reward and during reward-seeking, not only when pleasure occurs.' This distinction matters for understanding addiction (reward pathway = dopamine → nucleus accumbens). However, for AQA GCSE level, the simplified account is standard and not an error.
findings.verified_fact: Dopamine's role in the mesolimbic pathway (VTA → nucleus accumbens) is well-established as central to reward anticipation and reinforcement learning. At AQA GCSE level, 'dopamine = reward/pleasure neurotransmitter' is the expected formulation. Source: Schultz, W. (1998). Predictive reward signal of dopamine neurons. Journal of Neurophysiology, 80(1), 1–27.
findings.suggested_fix: No change required at GCSE level. Optional enhancement: 'Dopamine is involved in the brain's reward system — it is released during pleasurable experiences and reward-seeking behaviour, reinforcing the actions that led to the reward. This mechanism underlies addiction.'
